summary: Technical deep dive focused on autoscaling and capacity planning for AtlasPay's low-latency payment validation pipeline. Discussed burst policies, reserved GPU pools, queueing/backpressure models, KV cache warmup, batching strategies, and options for VPC/private deployment. Agreed on benchmarks and data share to size Dedicated capacity and to validate burst handling latency goals.
topics: autoscaling, burst policies, reserved GPUs, queueing models, backpressure, KV cache/prefix cache, batching, quantization effects, VPC/on-prem networking, SOC2 & KMS requirements
transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we can start; quick round of intros, alex redwood ae, priya our se who'll take the deep technical bits.
[00:18] Jordan: hey, jordan here. we run AtlasPay fraud+validation service, pretty sensitive to p99 latency, target <120ms on validation calls.
[00:32] Maya: maya, i look after ml infra; our traffic pattern is spiky - daily end of day batches plus random shopping spikes.
[00:45] Samir: samir, cto - i'm mostly here for architecture/ops questions.
[00:52] Priya: great, quick agenda: reserved capacity sizing, burst policy options (queueing vs immediate reject), KV cache warmup, batching tradeoffs, quantization impact, and VPC deployment constraints.
[01:15] Jordan: our big unknown is how many reserved gpus we need vs relying on burst; cost is a big factor.
[01:30] Priya: totally - we usually model a base reserved pool sized for steady qps and have burst pools for short spikes. decision drivers: acceptable p99 during bursts, budget for reserved commits, and cold-start tolerance.
[02:05] Maya: can you explain the queueing model - if we queue requests during burst, p99 might explode right?
[02:18] Priya: yes, queueing trades latency for throughput. we implement a hybrid: short-queue with per-tenant queue depth + dynamic rejections to protect SLOs. so e.g., 200ms soft queue window then fallback to lower-cost model or reject. this avoids infinite queuing.
[02:55] Alex: think of three levers - reserve, burst, and fallback. reserve gives predictable p99, burst handles short spikes (you pay extra), fallback can route to smaller model or cached response.
[03:24] Samir: what about KV cache - how quickly does it warm during scale-up? we can't afford long cold-cache periods.
[03:36] Priya: warmup depends on request locality and prefix reuse. for chat-like workloads with long context reuse kv cache hits are high. for stateless validation we see less reuse. we also offer proactive warmup: pre-populate cache on scale events using recent prefixes or synthetic warmup traces.
[04:05] Jordan: hmm, synthetic warmup sounds useful - does that add cost?
[04:12] Priya: small additional token cost but saves huge latency on first megas. you can also pin hot shards to reserved GPUs so their caches persist.
[04:33] Maya: pinning hot shards - is that per-customer?
[04:38] Priya: yes, in Dedicated you can pin model shards or keep a sticky set of GPUs for your tenant to keep kv in memory. that's typical for high-SLA customers.
[04:52] Jordan: let's talk numbers - we're seeing baseline 150 qps with bursts to 2k for 30-90s windows. what sizing do you recommend?
[05:05] Priya: rough back-of-envelope: if a single GPU handles ~200 qps for your model/profile at your target latency, you'd need 1 reserved to cover steady 150 qps (maybe 1 with some headroom). for 2k bursts you'd need 10 GPUs but we recommend a hybrid: reserve 2-3 GPUs and allow burst pool + autoscaler to spin up extra. with fast warmup and kv-cache pinning your p99 during bursts can be acceptable.
[05:45] Alex: also consider bin-packing - inference batch sizes and batching windows matter. if your requests are single-turn and low-latency we don't do long batching; but for micro-batching you get much better throughput.
[06:05] Maya: any guidance on batching window vs latency?
[06:10] Priya: small windows (2-10ms) often double throughput with minimal p99 impact for many workloads. bigger windows help throughput but hurt tail latency. we expose controls per-route.
[06:36] Jordan: quantization - does moving to 4-bit break accuracy for our fraud model?
[06:44] Priya: quantization tradeoffs are model-dependent. we run quantization-aware evals: 4-bit int8/4 configs can yield 5-8% quality delta on some models; for your score threshold-based validators that's sometimes acceptable, but for others we recommend mixed-precision or per-model evals first.
[07:15] Samir: what about fallback models during heavy burst - do you have auto-routing to smaller models?
[07:21] Priya: yes, smart routing allows policy-based fallback: route to quantized variant, smaller family, or cached response. you can set policy by latency budget and cost budget.
[07:37] Jordan: curious about autoscaling latency - how long to spin up new GPUs in Dedicated? we can't wait minutes during a 60s spike.
[07:48] Priya: we support two models: fast cold-burst using warm spare instances (warm pool) that are pre-allocated but not fully used - those can attach in ~20-40s; full cold scale (provisioning new cloud GPUs) can be minutes. warm pool is the typical approach for sub-minute spikes.
[08:20] Alex: this is why we recommend reserved + warm pool for predictable bursts. cost is higher but your p99 stays stable.
[08:33] Maya: what's the pricing delta for warm pool vs fully reserved?
[08:38] Alex: warm pool is typically charged like reserved but with a small premium when used; exact numbers in the sheet i'll send - depends on commit size and contract.
[08:50] Jordan: queueing policy again - do you do per-account priority to prevent noisy neighbors?
[08:57] Priya: yes, per-route and per-tenant priority and token-based quotas; we enforce backpressure and soft quotas. high-priority routes get kept alive in the queue longer.
[09:15] Samir: on VPC/on-prem: network latency to your control plane and to model instances - if we run private in a vpc in our region, what's the overhead?
[09:25] Priya: control plane calls are small; for private deployment we can deploy control plane in your VPC; inference traffic stays in VPC, so only local network latency affects you. we've seen <2ms overhead in most cloud regions. on-prem may see higher variability depending on NICs and interconnect.
[09:52] Maya: what about KMS for keys - we need CMEK/HSM.
[09:57] Alex: we support customer-managed keys (AWS KMS/GCP CMEK) and HSM integrations for Private deployments; we'll include our security docs.
[10:12] Jordan: ok good - SOC2 and audit logs are must-haves.
[10:16] Alex: we have SOC2 Type II, and retention options for audit logs; i'll share compliance pack.
[10:24] Priya: going back to capacity modeling: we usually ask for 7 days of traces and a SLAB (service-level arrival distribution) - that lets us simulate queueing, batching, and cache warmup to recommend reserve size + warm pool size.
[10:44] Jordan: we can provide traces but may need to strip PII.
[10:48] Alex: that's fine, sanitized traces work - we only need timing and prefix distributions.
[10:55] Maya: curious about burst policy examples - can we see a config?
[11:00] Priya: yes: example policy: reserve 3 gpus, warm_pool_min 2, burst_threshold 70% cpu, queue_window_ms 200, fallback to quantized-variant after 250ms queue. we can tune numbers per workload.
[11:23] Jordan: that queue_window_ms seems high - is 200ms acceptable for p99?
[11:29] Priya: 200ms is a soft window; if your p99 must be <120ms then you'd set shorter window and prefer warm_pool. it's a knobs tradeoff.
[11:43] Alex: also consider prefix caching to avoid full model run for common requests - that reduces load a lot.
[11:52] Maya: prefix caching effectiveness depends on request entropy; we'll share sample traces so you can estimate hit rates.
[12:01] Priya: another tactic is adaptive batching: during bursts we increase batch sizes on the fly where latency allows and reduce them as queues shrink, it's quite effective.
[12:18] Samir: any docs on cost modeling?
[12:22] Alex: yes, cost model spreadsheet I'll share - shows per-token, per-gpu-hour, warm_pool premia, and expected cost per 1k requests under different configs.
[12:35] Jordan: how about throttling strategy - would you prefer to reject or return degraded responses on overload?
[12:41] Priya: depends on client tolerance; we support reject with 429, degrade with cached/short-circuit responses, or return lower-quality model. It's pluggable per-route.
[12:56] Maya: for compliance we need audit of fallback decisions - is that logged?
[13:01] Alex: yes, all routing decisions and fallbacks are logged with trace ids. logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[13:12] Jordan: SE-specific question: can you pin KV cache to GPUs that are never evicted?
[13:18] Priya: we can reserve a shard and mark it sticky; eviction policies are configurable. in Dedicated you have more control.
[13:30] Maya: what about autoscale thresholds - can devs tune thresholds per-model?
[13:36] Priya: yes, thresholds are per-deployment: CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, observed p95/p99, custom metrics can trigger scale.
[13:48] Samir: we have regulatory windows where latency spikes are unacceptable. do you support scheduled capacity increases?
[13:55] Alex: yes - schedule scaling, pre-warm pools, or temporary commit increases for high-risk windows. we can also set calendar-based autoscale.
[14:10] Jordan: any pitfalls you've seen in similar customers?
[14:15] Priya: common ones: underestimating cache warmup time, relying solely on cold autoscale, not testing fallback correctness, and treating batching as a free perf boost without testing p99.
[14:33] Maya: good - we'll take those into account.
[14:38] Priya: next steps recap: we'll run a simulation with your traces, propose a reserve + warm_pool config, and run a small benchmark showing p50/p95/p99 and cost.
[14:51] Alex: i'll share pricing and compliance docs. priya will run bench. jordan will send traces. schedule follow up for private deployment demo.
[15:05] Samir: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[15:10] Jordan: thanks.
[15:12] Alex: thanks, end call.
